paras: The mock hanging of Dave Jackson took place in the county jail at Fort Worth, Texas, in the spring of 1882, when prisoners held a "kangaroo court," found Jackson, a Black prisoner, guilty, and strung him up to a rafter. He was nearly dead when he was cut down. A brief about the episode ran in newspapers across the South and in Ohio as a macabre curiosity.

On April 7, 1882, the Dallas Herald's Fort Worth correspondent reported that "Billie Jackson," a 19-year-old Black man, was accused of breaking into the room of Mr. Henderson's 15-year-old daughter south of the city and raping her, and that officers were on his track. Three days later the same correspondent wrote that "Dave Jackson the negro repist" had a preliminary hearing in the justice's court and was remanded to jail. As Jackson was taken back to jail, Henderson fired three shots at him, all of which missed; officers disarmed Henderson, a justice named McClung discharged him, and the correspondent reported "strong talk of mob violence."

According to a Fort Worth paper quoted in a widely reprinted brief, the prisoners in the county jail held a kangaroo court "the other day" and convicted "the negro Dave Jackson" after what the brief called an "exhaustive trial." When the foreman announced a verdict of guilty, the prisoners immediately strung Jackson up to a rafter, where he hung with his tongue protruding and his eyes rolled up. He was nearly dead when he was cut down, and the brief said that "little pains were taken to relieve him." The brief names no charge for the mock trial, gives no date, and does not say whether jailers intervened.

No report of any action against the prisoners appears in the coverage. On May 5 the grand jury at Fort Worth returned an indictment against "Bill Jackson" for rape, and on October 19 a jury sentenced Bill Jackson to 90 years for the rape of Miss Florence Henderson, described as white. The same jail and charge suggest that Billie, Bill and Dave Jackson were one man, but the papers never tie the rape case to the mock hanging.

The hanging reached readers only through a short item in "Southern Gleanings" columns, set among notes on crops, a 200-year-old gourd and the price of Tallahassee's old gas works. It ran on May 4 in the Bolivar Bulletin in Tennessee and on May 6 in the Milan Exchange, the Huntsville Gazette, the Grenada Sentinel and the Panola Weekly Star. The Highland Weekly News of Hillsboro, Ohio, printed it on May 11 with one word changed, saying little pains were taken to "revive" him.

The brief treated the episode as theater, calling it "terribly realistic acting" and the prisoners' "grim pastime," and said the scene lacked only "the black cap and the coffin to make a hideous forecast of a coming event." It did not criticize the prisoners or the jail. The Dallas Herald, which followed the rape case from Fort Worth and called Jackson "the guilty brute" before any trial, carried no report of the mock hanging.

bases: Fellow prisoners in the Fort Worth county jail staged a mock trial of a Black prisoner and hanged him from a rafter until he was nearly dead, but did not kill him (A3).

Jackson was 'nearly dead when cut down' but survived as far as the brief reports, so no one was killed; the hanging followed a mock 'kangaroo court' verdict by 'the prisoners', a group of unstated number (A3).
Every report of the hanging is the same unattributed 'Southern Gleanings' brief, citing an unnamed Fort Worth 'local paper' (A3, A5-A9); no independent account was found.
